chapter: New York, church bands and early training
title: Edmund Jenkins urges more study; the $5 lesson with Dumont
summary: Jenkins in London suggested he continue studying; Briggs recalls his single paid lessons with the Hippodrome trumpeter Dumont and comments on what lessons cost.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: You see, they had background, they knew what they were doing. Today, if you can't arrange, if you don't know your keys, all your keys, you can't be a professor, you can't teach. You have to know everything in order to teach pupils. And that the majority didn't have. And I was fortunate when I went to London with Mr. Cook with the orchestra, through Mr. Jenkins, I shall never forget Edmund Jenkins, regardless of his Dad, God bless his soul -- Edmund Jenkins came over to the
Briggs

Syncopated Orchestra, and he knew the other two other boys, one a trumpet and the other a trombone, it was the thing they got along pretty nicely, and after -- I'm not trying to throw flowers at myself. But he probably thought that -- he heard the orchestra, he heard me play and he thought that I needed a helping hand, you see.

So, he suggested to me, he said, "Would you like to continue your studies?" I said, "Sure, I certainly will." I said, "Gee, I had a teacher in New York, he was a Frenchman, he was the first trumpet player at the Hippodrome Theater."
I was recommended to him, and I had one lesson, first lesson, $5.00.
In those days --
It was a lot of money.
A whole family of ten people could live almost a month. (Laughter).
(Laughter).
Briggs

That was my little savings from my dance schools, you know, and gigs and things, playing more or less, twice, as I said, almost twice a week, I replaced Dewitt Martin who was an excellent cornet player. Excellent, but he was always drunk. You see. And it was through my savings and everything, that I managed to pay. I took two lessons. I went back a second time. Because I went to hear him play at the Hippodrome Theater and he was a very fine cornet player -- trumpet player.
Well, the Hippodrome Theater was where?
Well, look, it was the last place I played with Noble Sissle's orchestra in 1931 before we came over, came back the last time.
Right.
I'm trying to think of where it's at, 'cause one of my, -- what do you call -- brother-in-law -- what do you call
Briggs
him, he's not a brother-in-law, he married one of my nieces. He heard me at the Hippodrome Theater with Noble Sissle's orchestra in 1930, and I'm trying to think -- it was around Broadway somewhere.
Broadway somewhere.
It was in midtown, yes, midtown.
Well, this teacher of yours was white then?
Yes, Mr. Dumont, yes. Yes, he was white. I didn't think much of him for charging that price.

I had two good lessons, really two good lessons, but in those days, a lesson shouldn't cost -- didn't cost, -- I mean, if you get the best professor on earth in New York, it wouldn't be over $1.00. In those days.
Right.
You see. Uptown, colored professors give you a lesson, whatever
Briggs
they can do, for about $.50. Yes, I see.
$.25. But a real teacher was a dollar. Why at the Martin Smith School, they couldn't pay that kind of money.
No, sure.
